ASUS ProArt PA27UCGE is a 27-inch 4K monitor with several standout features in a competitive display market. First, it supports up to a 160Hz refresh rate, making it easy to handle web scrolling, gaming, and video editing. Additionally, it ships with an optional monitor hood to reduce ambient light interference, and features a built-in motorized calibrator for periodic color calibration.

We previously reviewed ASUS's 5K ProArt (review) and 6K ProArt displays (review), both of which are highly cost-effective third-party options for Mac users. So how does this ProArt display, with slightly lower resolution but more extra features, perform? See our video review for details.

The ASUS ProArt display series has always focused on photo editing and video production, and this 27-inch 4K PA27UCGE is no exception. Although it cannot deliver the rich, deep blacks of OLED technology, its 600-nit IPS panel provides excellent contrast and sustained brightness, making it ideal for working in environments where lighting cannot be fully controlled.

Video: ASUS 4K 160Hz Monitor—Worth Buying?

The PA27UCGE supports variable refresh rates up to 160Hz at 4K resolution. This not only makes text scrolling smoother, but is also great for high-frame-rate video production and gaming. I tested it alongside a 16-inch MacBook Pro with 120Hz ProMotion, and the two displays had matching refresh rates, making for a very smooth experience. Even when just connecting an M4 Mac mini to a single display, support for 120Hz, 144Hz, or even 160Hz is quite practical.

Although I generally prefer glossy screens over matte coatings, this monitor's anti-glare, low-reflectivity "LuxPixel" coating effectively reduces reflections while maintaining text clarity, avoiding the text blurring commonly seen on typical matte displays. It's worth noting that text sharpness is still affected to some extent, but this is the best-performing matte display I have used—second only to screens using nano-etch technology (such as Apple's matte option).

The PA27UCGE also comes with an optional monitor hood to help block ambient light reflections. I found the hood installation process a bit cumbersome, and its design and build quality feel somewhat clumsy, but once installed, it does effectively block ambient light from hitting the screen surface.

macOS Scaling Settings

A major drawback of using a 4K display with macOS is the inability to achieve perfect native 1:1 scaling at the HiDPI 2880×1440 resolution that most users expect at this screen size. As with all 4K displays, when the display is set to 2560×1440 in macOS, the system first renders to a virtual 5120×2880 canvas, then scales down fractionally to a pixel-doubled 1440p "retina" HiDPI resolution. The result is very close to a true 5K panel, but since it isn't perfect 1:1 scaling, text sharpness is slightly reduced.

Using the native pixel-doubled 1920×1080 resolution achieves true 1:1 scaling with extremely sharp text, but at the cost of significantly reduced workspace. For most people, sacrificing a bit of sharpness for more screen real estate is a worthwhile trade-off, but it's worth noting. When my eyesight was better, I was more sensitive to this issue, but as I've gotten older, these differences have become easier to accept.

Color Calibration Measurement Results

The motorized calibrator is built in beneath the logo on the bottom bezel, allowing the ProArt 4K to calibrate colors automatically without the need for external calibration tools or software, resulting in more accurate colors. However, I personally still prefer using an external tool like the Calibrite Display Pro HL for greater flexibility.

The built-in motorized calibrator can be calibrated via the OSD, but to view actual data, you need to install the Asus ProArt Calibration tool. The fixed position of the built-in calibrator is a major limitation, but its biggest advantage is the ability to schedule automatic calibration when the display is idle. Since the calibration process can take over 30 minutes, this feature is very useful in the long run.

According to the included calibration report, this unit has an average Delta-E of 0.78 for sRGB and 1.12 for DCI-P3—both excellent. This value measures the difference between the original input color and the color actually displayed by the screen, so the lower the value, the higher the color accuracy. In my experience, a value below 2 is considered ideal.

ASUS claims the PA27UCGE has 98% DCI-P3 color gamut coverage, making it ideal for color grading and video editing in Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve. To verify ASUS's claims, I tested using both the built-in calibrator and Calibrate Display Pro HL, paired with Calibrate's Profiler software and ASUS's own ProArt calibration tool.

The measurements showed an average DCI-P3 Delta E below 1.2, very close to ASUS's claimed figures. DCI-P3 color gamut coverage was also quite accurate. When editing and color grading Canon Log 2 footage shot on a Canon R5 Mark II in Final Cut Pro, overall colors were largely accurate.

More importantly, this display performs well in color and brightness uniformity, with brightness deviations below 5 in nearly all Calibrite Profiler tests. In terms of brightness, ASUS rates it at 600 nits, but I measured peak brightness exceeding 700 nits during testing.

Design, Build Quality, and Ergonomics

The ASUS ProArt 4K monitor continues ASUS's established design language, and like the previous 5K and 6K ProArt monitors, its build quality is unlikely to win any awards. This doesn't mean ASUS's build quality is poor—rather, Apple invests heavily in this area, so its displays almost always have higher production standards.

Third-party display makers generally don't compete with Apple in this regard. Instead, they typically offer better value through cheaper, plastic-heavy, mass-producible housings.

In short, of course I would prefer the ASUS monitor to feature a unibody aluminum chassis with smooth, well-balanced adjustment design, but the reality is that finding a third-party display maker willing to go head-to-head with Apple in this area is quite difficult. ASUS compensates with a richer overall feature set, higher refresh rate, and more I/O options.

Ergonomics

From an ergonomic standpoint, the ASUS ProArt 4K offers fairly comprehensive adjustment options. The display can tilt +23 or -5 degrees, swivel 90 degrees left or right, pivot ±30 degrees horizontally, and provides 120mm of height adjustment. The smoothness and balance of adjustments fall short of the Apple Studio Display. Apple's base Studio Display offers tilt adjustment, while the tilt- and height-adjustable stand costs an extra $200, but completely lacks swivel and pivot functions.

Overall, the ASUS PA27UCGE leans more toward practical than aesthetic in design, build quality, and ergonomics. Of course, I would love to have a clean, logo- and button-free front bezel design like the Studio Display, but considering this ASUS 4K monitor is only $800, its value is undeniable.

Ports

While Apple has added Thunderbolt 5 daisy-chaining to the new Studio Display, third-party monitors like the PA27UCGE offer a richer set of connectivity options.

The USB 3.2 Gen 1 upstream port is the primary interface most Mac users use to connect their MacBook or Mac mini. For laptop users, the USB upstream port can deliver up to 96W of power, enough to fully charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro. The PA27UCGE also features dual HDMI 2.1 ports and one DisplayPort 1.4 input, suitable for connecting PCs, game consoles, or set-top boxes like Apple TV.

  • Digital Inputs: 1 x DisplayPort v1.4 2 x HDMI 2.1 1 x DisplayPort over USB Type-C
  • USB Ports: 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 upstream Type-C (data only) 1 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 downstream Type-C 2 x USB 3.2 Gen 1 downstream Type-A
  • Audio: Headphone jack Built-in speakers (2W x 2)

In addition to the built-in USB hub, the display also supports automatic KVM functionality, allowing you to easily connect two computers simultaneously and share one set of mouse and keyboard.

9to5Mac's Take

The ASUS ProArt PA27UCGE offers exceptional value for its price. It features excellent DCI-P3 color gamut support, ideal for photo and video editing, while offering a high refresh rate that pairs perfectly with the ProMotion-equipped MacBook Pro.

The LuxPixel matte screen reduces reflections without overly compromising text clarity, and while the included monitor hood isn't the most elegant design, it effectively blocks ambient light.

Not to be overlooked, this display offers rich input support, including dual HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB-C, with hub and KVM functionality.

As with most third-party displays on the market, its build quality can't match Apple's own displays, but this is a near-universal issue with third-party products. In compensation, it offers richer ergonomic adjustments than Apple.

ASUS provides a 3-year warranty for ProArt displays (including the PA27UCGE), extendable by 2 years for free upon registration, for a total of 5 years of coverage. Considering that most displays on the market (including Apple products) only come with a 1-year warranty, 5 years of coverage is extremely attractive.

It's certainly not perfect, but at $800, this ASUS ProArt 4K monitor delivers performance far above its price point. For video editors or gamers seeking a high-refresh-rate external display, I absolutely recommend this product.

What do you think? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments below.
